questions.question: A patient has Streptococcus pneumoniae community-acquired pneumonia with the following MICs: penicillin 2, erythromycin 64, clindamycin 256.
questions.question_raw: Strep pneumonia CAP with MICs as follows: Pen 2; Erythro 64; Clinda 256

parts.text: Is it safe to use penicillin? Why or why not?
What is the mechanism of penicillin resistance in pneumococcus?
What are 2 types of macrolide resistance?
What type is present here?

parts_raw.text: Is it safe to use penicillin? Why or why not?
B.  What is the mechanism of pen resistance in pneumococcus?
C. What are 2 types of macrolide resistance?
d) What type is present here?

questions.model_answer:
a) Yes, for this non-CNS infection treated parenterally. Current breakpoints define a pneumococcus as penicillin-susceptible if the MIC is <=2 ug/mL for non-CNS parenteral therapy, so an MIC of 2 is susceptible IV. (It would be intermediate/resistant by the oral non-CNS breakpoint of <=0.06 and resistant by the CNS breakpoint of <=0.06, so it could not be used orally or for meningitis.)
b) Alteration of penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs): mutations in the genes encoding PBPs (notably PBP2b for low-level and PBP2x/1a for high-level resistance) reduce penicillin's binding affinity. These altered genes are acquired by transformation (e.g., from S. mitis).
c) (1) Ribosomal target methylation encoded by ermB (methylates A2058 in domain V of 23S rRNA), giving high-level resistance (>=64 ug/mL) and the MLSB phenotype. (2) Efflux encoded by mefA, giving lower-level resistance (usually <=16 ug/mL), affecting macrolides only.
d) MLSB (ermB-mediated ribosomal methylation): resistance to both the macrolide (erythromycin 64) and clindamycin (256) indicates ribosomal methylation, not an efflux pump (which would spare clindamycin).

cohort_answer.text:
IV Non-meningitic: ≤2 is susceptible --- can use; Po pen: ≤0.06 µg/mL (same breakpoints as meningitis); Meningitic: pen susceptible is ≤0.06 µg/mL, resistant is ≥0.12 µg/mL
Alteration of target enzymes (PBPs)
Efflux pumps (mef in strep pneumo, mSRA in staph aureus), resistance to macrolides, not clinda (M phenotype); Target site alteration by methylation of ribosome to prevent drug binding, resistance to both macrolides, lincosamides, streptogamins (MLSB)
Target site alteration MLSB

questions.model_answer:
a) The Etest MIC is read at the point where the elliptical zone of inhibition intersects the graded strip: penicillin 0.5 ug/mL and ceftriaxone 0.06 ug/mL.
b) Because this is CSF, apply the CNS (meningitis) breakpoints. Penicillin: susceptible <=0.06, resistant >0.06 ug/mL, so MIC 0.5 = RESISTANT. Ceftriaxone: susceptible <=0.5 ug/mL, so MIC 0.06 = SUSCEPTIBLE. Report the organism as penicillin-resistant, ceftriaxone-susceptible for meningitis; empiric vancomycin plus ceftriaxone/cefotaxime is warranted until confirmed.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Smoking (current cigarette use) and heavy alcohol use. (2) Living or working conditions with crowding or outbreak risk - shelters, correctional facilities, long-term care, daycare exposure, Indigenous community residence. (3) Illicit drug use, homelessness, and prior invasive pneumococcal disease or recurrent pneumonia. (4) Prior pneumococcal vaccination history, plus cochlear implant, CSF leak, or basilar skull fracture/head trauma.
b) Nephrotic syndrome is a high-risk condition. Give one dose of conjugate vaccine PCV20 alone (single dose completes the series). If PCV13 is used instead, follow with PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later, and give a single PPSV23 booster 5 years after the first PPSV23 for this high-risk condition.

questions.model_answer:
a) Alteration of penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) with reduced affinity for penicillin, due to mutations in PBP genes (PBP2b for low-level, PBP2x/1a for high-level resistance) acquired by transformation.
b) Yes, if given IV for this non-CNS infection: MIC <=2 ug/mL is susceptible by the non-CNS parenteral breakpoint. It could not be used orally (oral non-CNS susceptible <=0.06) or for CNS infection.
c) Two mechanisms: ermB-encoded ribosomal methylation of 23S rRNA (high-level resistance >=64, MLSB phenotype) and mefA-encoded efflux pump (lower-level resistance <=16, macrolides only).
d) MLSB (ermB ribosomal methylation): high-level resistance to both erythromycin AND clindamycin indicates methylation rather than an efflux pump.

cohort_answer.text: Penicillin: Mechanism of resistance: altered enzyme structure (PBP) with reduced affinity for the antibiotic. Can be used if IV completely (MIC ≤2). If oral (or CNS infection), cannot use it. Macrolides and Clindamycin: Most likely mechanism is ermB (methylation of ribosome binding site). This gives high level resistance to macrolides and clindamycin (MLSB phenotype). Another mechanism of resistance is mefA (efflux pump), which is low level resistance, but this does not generally impact clindamycin

questions.question: What are the indications for pneumococcal vaccination and the appropriate regimens?

parts.text: What are the indications for pneumococcal vaccination (and appropriate regimens)?

parts_raw.text: What are the indications for pneumococcal vaccination (and appropriate regimens)?

questions.model_answer:
Indications (ACIP, per Table 199.7): (1) all adults aged >=65 years; (2) immunocompetent adults 19-64 with chronic conditions - chronic heart disease, chronic lung disease, diabetes, alcoholism, chronic liver disease/cirrhosis, cigarette smoking, CSF leak, cochlear implant; (3) functional/anatomic asplenia (sickle cell, splenectomy); (4) immunocompromising conditions - congenital/acquired immunodeficiency, HIV, chronic renal failure/nephrotic syndrome, leukemia/lymphoma/Hodgkin/generalized malignancy/multiple myeloma, iatrogenic immunosuppression, solid organ transplant; plus routine childhood immunization.
Regimens: Children - PCV13 at 2, 4, 6 months with a booster at 12-15 months. Adults >=65 vaccine-naive - PCV13 first, then PPSV23 6-12 months later. Adults 19-64 with chronic conditions - a single dose of PPSV23. Adults with immunocompromise, asplenia, CSF leak or cochlear implant - PCV13 first, then PPSV23 >=8 weeks later, with PPSV23 revaccination 5 years after the first PPSV23 dose (and, for age <65 groups, a final dose at 65).

cohort_answer.text: Indications: routine infant/child immunization, catch-up for missed doses, high risk of IPD due to underlying medical conditions, LTC facility residents, adults 65+, high risk lifestyle factors (smokers, alcoholism, homeless), consider for illicit drug users. Regimens: Age >=65 immunocompetent - PPV23 x1 dose; high risk children 2-18 - PCV-13 followed by PPV-23 >=8 weeks later; high risk adults - one dose PPV-23; boosters for high-risk >=5 years after initial; HSCT adults - 3 doses PCV-13 4 weeks apart starting 3-9 months post-transplant, PPV-23 given 12-18 months post-transplant

questions.question: For Streptococcus pneumoniae, describe the 2 mechanisms of macrolide resistance: name the 2 genes and state whether each includes clindamycin resistance.

parts.text: Fill in the chart on macrolide resistance mechanisms (mechanism, gene, includes clindamycin or not).

parts_raw.text: Fill in the chart on macrolide resistance mechanisms

questions.model_answer:
Background: macrolides bind a pocket of the 23S subunit of the 50S ribosome at domain V of the peptidyl transferase loop, blocking protein assembly.
(1) Ribosomal target methylation - gene ermB - methylates base A2058 in domain V of 23S rRNA, altering the pocket; high-level resistance (>=64 ug/mL); MLSB phenotype, so it DOES include clindamycin (plus lincosamides and streptogramin B).
(2) Efflux pump - gene mefA - extrudes the macrolide; lower-level resistance (usually <=16 ug/mL); affects macrolides ONLY, does NOT include clindamycin.

cohort_answer.text: Macrolides insert into a pocket of the 23S subunit of the 50S ribosome, attaching at domain V of the peptidyl transferase loop, blocking protein assembly. mefA-encoded efflux pumps: pump that extrudes macrolides, low level resistance MIC<16, affects macrolide resistance only. ermB-encoded methylases: alter the ribosomal binding site, high level resistance MIC>64, MLSB phenotype - inducible resistance to Macrolide/Lincosamide/Streptogramin B (includes clindamycin).

questions.model_answer:
a) Alteration of penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) with decreased penicillin affinity, from mutations in PBP genes (notably PBP2x and PBP1a, also PBP2b), acquired by transformation from other streptococci.
b) Yes, for this non-CNS infection given parenterally: penicillin MIC <=2 ug/mL is susceptible by the non-CNS parenteral breakpoint (ceftriaxone MIC 1 is also non-CNS susceptible). It could not be used orally or for meningitis.

cohort_answer.text: a) Alteration of PBPs through mutations of PBP genes, particularly PBP2X and PBP1A (mutated genetic material transferred via transformation). b) Yes - for infections other than CSF, MIC<=2ug/mL is considered susceptible for parenteral penicillin. c) Ribosomal methylation (ermB gene, methylates base in 23S rRNA, alters ribosomal pocket); efflux pump (mefA gene). d) mefA gene acquisition (lower level resistance, MIC<=16) as opposed to ermB (high level resistance, MIC>=64).

questions.model_answer: (1) Optochin (ethylhydrocupreine) susceptibility - S. pneumoniae is optochin-sensitive (zone of inhibition around the disk), distinguishing it from most viridans streptococci. (2) Bile solubility - pneumococcal colonies are lysed by bile salts (autolysin-mediated), whereas other alpha-hemolytic streptococci are not; positive bile solubility is specific for S. pneumoniae. (Adjuncts: Quellung/capsular swelling reaction, catalase-negative, MALDI-TOF.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Optochin susceptibility and bile solubility are standard clinical-microbiology identification tests (e.g., Mandell diagnostic microbiology / CLSI); the read chapter slice describes the Quellung reaction but not these confirmatory tests.

cohort_answer.text: Optochin sensitive (can also be seen with other strep species); Bile soluble (only S. pneumo; bile salt lyses pneumococcal cell wall) (speaker notes: Optochin +, Bile solubility +, Bile esculin -, MALDI)

parts.text: Is it safe to use penicillin? Why or why not?

parts_raw.text: A) Is it safe to use penicillin? Why or why not?

questions.model_answer: a) Yes. This is a non-CNS infection (pneumonia) and penicillin will be given parenterally. By current CLSI breakpoints for parenteral penicillin in non-CNS pneumococcal infection, susceptible is defined as MIC ≤2 µg/mL; intermediate >2 and ≤4; resistant >4. An MIC of 2 therefore falls in the susceptible range, and pneumococcal pneumonia caused by susceptible (or even intermediately resistant) strains responds to penicillin. (Note: this same MIC of 2 would be resistant if the infection were meningitis, where the susceptible breakpoint is ≤0.06 µg/mL.)

cohort_answer.text: Yes. MIC less than or equal to 2 is susceptible for non-CNS infection

parts.text: What is the mechanism of penicillin resistance in pneumococcus?

parts_raw.text: B) What is the mechanism of pen resistance in pneumococcus?

questions.model_answer: a) Penicillin resistance results from altered penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), the peptidoglycan-synthesis enzymes (1a, 1b, 2a, 2b, 2x, 3) that penicillin normally binds covalently. Mutations in the genes encoding these enzymes reduce penicillin's binding affinity: alterations in PBP2b tend to give low-level resistance, whereas mutations in PBP2x are associated with high-level resistance (and PBP2x/1a changes also confer third-generation cephalosporin resistance). Pneumococci acquire these altered genes by transformation — uptake of naked DNA from other bacteria in close proximity (e.g., the PBP2b sequence in many resistant isolates was acquired from Streptococcus mitis).

cohort_answer.text: PBP alteration in binding affinity (PBP2X). Acquired through transformation (acquiring naked DNA from other dying bacteria). [From Mandell's: six PBP enzymes 1A,1B,2A,2B,2X,3; alterations in PBP2B more likely low-level resistance, mutations in PBP2X associated with high-level resistance; pneumococci acquire resistance genes by transformation, e.g. from S. mitis]

parts.text: What is the empiric therapy for community-acquired meningitis in a healthy 45-year-old?
What if the ceftriaxone MIC is 2? Give two options for treatment.
What follow-up test is indicated?

parts_raw.text: A. What is the empiric therapy for community acquired meningitis in a healthy 45 yo.?
B.  What if CTX MIC is 2?  Give two options for Rx.
C.  What follow up test is indicated?

questions.model_answer:
a) Vancomycin (30-45 mg/kg/day IV divided q8-12h, trough 15-20) PLUS a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h or cefotaxime 8-12 g/day divided q4-6h), with adjunctive dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h given 20-30 min before or with the first antibiotic dose. Vancomycin covers S. pneumoniae with reduced ceftriaxone susceptibility (MIC >=2).
b) A pneumococcus with ceftriaxone MIC >=1.0 requires combination therapy: (1) vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime); (2) vancomycin plus moxifloxacin. Because the ceftriaxone MIC >2, add rifampin (if susceptible) and it is especially important to document CSF sterility.
c) Repeat lumbar puncture at 36-48 h to confirm CSF sterility, since the cefotaxime/ceftriaxone MIC is >2.0 and the patient is on adjunctive dexamethasone.

cohort_answer.text:
CTX/vanco
MIC =>1 = non susceptible. Meropenem, CTX and Vanco, Moxifloxacin
Repeat lumbar puncture

questions.question: Bacterial meningitis.
questions.question_raw: Bacterial meningitis

parts.text: What are the empiric options for treatment of pneumococcus based on MIC?

parts_raw.text: What are the empiric options for treatment of pneumococcus based on MIC?

questions.model_answer:
Pneumococcal therapy by CLSI meningitis breakpoints:
(1) Penicillin MIC <=0.06 (susceptible): penicillin G or ampicillin.
(2) Penicillin MIC >=0.12 (resistant) with ceftriaxone/cefotaxime MIC <1.0: a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime); alternative meropenem or cefepime.
(3) Ceftriaxone/cefotaxime MIC >=1.0: vancomycin PLUS a third-generation cephalosporin; alternative vancomycin plus moxifloxacin.
Add rifampin if the cefotaxime/ceftriaxone MIC is >4.0 (or if response is delayed), and only when the isolate is rifampin-susceptible. Typical duration 10-14 days.

cohort_answer.text: Penicillin MIC (meningitis) <0.06: use penicillin (R: ≥0.12). Ceftriaxone (meningitis) MIC: S ≤0.5: use ceftriaxone. CTX >1: treat with CTX 2g q12h and Vanco 15-20mg/kg q8h. Rifampin added if CTX >2. Duration 10-14 days

questions.model_answer:
a) Vancomycin (30-45 mg/kg/day IV divided q8-12h) plus a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h or cefotaxime), with adjunctive dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h started with or just before the first antibiotic dose.

questions.model_answer: a) Neisseria meningitidis — terminal complement blockade by eculizumab confers a >300/100,000 risk of meningococcal disease. b) Mycobacterium tuberculosis (reactivation TB) — B-cell depletion plus latent infection in an immigrant from an endemic region. c) Streptococcus pneumoniae — humoral/antibody deficiency of myeloma predisposes to encapsulated pneumococcal pneumonia. d) Capnocytophaga canimorsus — fulminant sepsis after a dog bite in an asplenic host.

questions.question: Community-acquired meningitis in an otherwise healthy 45-year-old man.
questions.question_raw:
Q2 (2015, 2013 PM)
Community-acquired meningitis in an otherwise healthy 45M.

parts.text: What is the empiric treatment?
Streptococcus pneumoniae on culture with penicillin MIC 4 and ceftriaxone MIC 1 - what are two treatments? What if the ceftriaxone MIC is 2? Give two options for treatment.
What should you do in follow-up?

parts_raw.text: a) What is empiric tx?
b) Strep pneumo on culture with pen MIC 4, CTX MIC 1, what are two treatments? What if CTX MIC is 2? Give 2 options for tx?
c) What should you do in follow-up?

questions.model_answer:
a) Vancomycin (30-45 mg/kg/day IV divided q8-12h, trough 15-20) plus a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h or cefotaxime 8-12 g/day divided q4-6h), with adjunctive dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg q6h given 20-30 min before or with the first antibiotic dose.
b) Ceftriaxone MIC 1 (>=1.0): (1) vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin; (2) vancomycin plus moxifloxacin. Ceftriaxone MIC 2: the same two options - (1) vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin and (2) vancomycin plus moxifloxacin - and add rifampin if CTX MIC >4 or response is delayed. Meropenem is an alternative only when the ceftriaxone MIC is <1.0, not for high-MIC strains.
c) Repeat lumbar puncture at 36-48 h to document CSF sterility, mandatory when the cefotaxime/ceftriaxone MIC is >2.0 or the patient is not improving, especially on adjunctive dexamethasone.
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort lists meropenem as an option for ceftriaxone MIC 2; per Table 87.13 meropenem is an alternative only when the ceftriaxone MIC is <1.0, so the MIC-2 options are vancomycin plus a cephalosporin or vancomycin plus moxifloxacin.

cohort_answer.text:
a) Vancomycin (35 to 45 mg/kg/day divided into doses every 8 or 12 h) + third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h). Vanco for the possibility of S. pneumoniae with reduced susceptibility to ceftriaxone (MIC ≥2 µg/mL). Steroids: Because CNS infections can be complicated by cerebral edema and increased ICP --> can give steroids. Give just before (20 min) or with the FIRST dose of abx. Improves outcomes in kids w/ H. influenzae type b, and perhaps pneumococcal meningitis, and in adults with pneumococcal meningitis. Once the first dose of antibiotic has been given, starting dexamethasone is no longer advocated by the 2004 IDSA guidelines, but it is recommended based on expert opinion up to 4 hours after starting antibiotics in the 2016 European guidelines and up to 12 hours in the 2016 UK guidelines. Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h if possibility of encephalitis clinically (but not necessary for HSV meningitis).

b) Penicillin: Intermediate susceptiblity 0.1 to 1.0 µg/mL; Highly resistant when higher than 2.0 µg/mL; CLSI breakpoints of 0.06 µg/mL and lower for susceptible, 0.12µg/mL and higher for resistant. Alteration of PBP. Some serotypes specifically: mostly 6, 14, 19 and 23. 3rd gen cephalosporins (Cefotaxime, Ceftriaxone): Resistance with MIC more than 2µg/mL; When 1µg/mL or less, successful treatment with high-dose 3rd gen Cephalosporin. Vancomycin: Usually used with Cephalosporin; Associated with tolerant strains; Need adjunctive dexamethasone to achieve appropriate CSF concentration. Meropenem: Outcomes similar to cephalosporins - possible agent; Not an alternative for pneumococcal isolates highly resistant to penicillin and cephalosporins. Newer Fluoroquinolones (Moxifloxacin, Gemifloxacin, Gatifloxacin, Garenoxacin): Good in vitro activity; Comparable outcomes when compared with ceftriaxone; Decreased susceptibility, mostly to Levofloxacin. Regimen given: Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h PLUS vancomycin IV (trough 15 - 20). 2nd Line: Meropenem 2g IV q8h. 2nd line: Moxifloxacin 400 mg PO q24h. For CTX MIC 2: Meropenem; Moxifloxacin.

c) Repeat LP - 36 to 48h of therapy: any patient who is not improving as expected within 48 hours of therapy, or pneumococcal isolate for which the cefotaxime/ceftriaxone MIC is greater than 2.0 µg/mL (this may be especially important for patients who are receiving adjunctive dexamethasone therapy). Hearing screening and neurodevelopmental follow-up. Vaccination for meningococcal + pneumococcus. Post-exposure prophylaxis. No more details on adult follow up anywhere (not in CID, Mandell, uptodate). [Additional notes: Consider vaccination with Prevnar and pneumovax; Hearing screen (in children – developmental followup); Immunoglobulins, HIV serology; For kids – test for Sickle Cell; Duration of tx for pneumococcal meningitis is 10-14 days; Repeat LP (repeat CSF cx) if: No improvement by 48h of tx, 2-3 d after tx start organism found to be resistant, Persistent fever > 8 days without another explanation, Neonatal gram negative meningitis, CSF shunt infections.]

questions.question: Antibacterial mechanisms of resistance. State the mechanism of resistance for each organism/antibiotic pair: Klebsiella pneumoniae to meropenem; Pseudomonas aeruginosa to meropenem; Enterococcus faecium to penicillin; Enterococcus faecalis with high-level aminoglycoside resistance; Streptococcus pneumoniae to moxifloxacin; Streptococcus pyogenes to erythromycin.
questions.question_raw: Q46 (2010 AM, 2009 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance (fill in the blank table): K. pneumoniae with Meropenem; P. aeruginosa with Meropenem; E faecium with penicillin; E faecalis with high level aminoglycoside resistance; S. pneumoniae with moxifloxacin; S. pyogenes with erythromycin

parts.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each organism/antibiotic pair.

parts_raw.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each organism/antibiotic pair

questions.model_answer:
(1) K. pneumoniae/meropenem: carbapenemase production - Ambler class A KPC (most common), class B metallo-beta-lactamases (NDM, VIM, IMP), class D OXA-48-type; also ESBL/AmpC plus porin loss (OmpK35/OmpK36).
(2) P. aeruginosa/meropenem: loss/downregulation of the OprD porin (with basal AmpC); acquired metallo-beta-lactamases (VIM, IMP); upregulated MexAB-OprM efflux (affects mero/dori but not imipenem).
(3) E. faecium/penicillin: overproduction of a low-affinity penicillin-binding protein PBP5 (altered target).
(4) E. faecalis/high-level aminoglycoside resistance: acquired aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme, classically the bifunctional AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2'')-Ia.
(5) S. pneumoniae/moxifloxacin: stepwise target mutations in the quinolone-resistance-determining regions of gyrA (DNA gyrase) and parC (topoisomerase IV).
(6) S. pyogenes/erythromycin: ribosomal methylation of 23S rRNA by an erm-encoded methylase (MLSB phenotype), or macrolide efflux via mef.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mechanisms are from Mandell Ch. 18 (antimicrobial resistance) / standard microbiology, not this Enterobacteriaceae chapter.

cohort_answer.text: K. pneumoniae/Meropenem: Ambler class D oxacillinases (OXAs); acquired class B beta-lactamases (VIM, NDM); Ambler Class A KPCs; reduced expression of OmpK35/OmpK36. P. aeruginosa/Meropenem: downregulated/absent OprD porin with background AmpC; MBLs (VIM, IMP, SPM-1 less common); upregulation of MexA-MexB-OprM efflux (resistant to mero/doripenem but not imipenem). E. faecium/Penicillin: altered PBPs (resistant pbp5 allele). E. faecalis/HLAR: bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-IE-APH(2'')-Ia. S. pneumoniae/Moxifloxacin: dual mutations in GyrA and ParC. S. pyogenes/Erythromycin: erm gene (ribosome methylation) - methylase enzymes dimethylate adenine on 23S rRNA of 50S subunit, disrupting MLS binding.
